Hybrid Reasoning Agents

Jiaru Zou Affiliation: Stanford University    Yunzhe Qi Affiliation: UIUC    Sirui Chen    Federico Bianchi Affiliation: Together AI    Shang Zhu Affiliation: Together AI    Pan Lu Affiliation: Stanford University    Jingrui He Affiliation: UIUC    James Zou Affiliation: Stanford University Affiliation: Together AI Affiliation: Meta Affiliation: Project Lead Affiliation: Core Contributor
Abstract

How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent’s continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%–54.7% token reduction, 1.8×\times–2.6×\times faster inference, and 2.7×\times–3.7×\times cost savings.

1 Introduction

Frontier intelligence no longer scales through the model’s reasoning alone, but depends increasingly on its ability to interact with the external world (Team, 2026; Kwa et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026). To solve a hard problem, an LLM agent must reach beyond the model itself by continually invoking specialized tools, observing feedback from the environment, and adapting its next move (Qu et al., 2025; Silver and Sutton, 2025; Feng et al., 2026). Beneath this expanding repertoire of agent harnesses lies a single lingua franca: text, the common medium of both the agent’s autoregressive generation and its environment interaction (Sumers et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026b). All intermediate reasoning trajectories are generated token by token as text before the agent can act on the environment.

A separate line of work on latent reasoning points in a different direction (Zhu et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2025). By unfolding computation directly in continuous hidden space, latent models bypass the need to decode and verbalize every intermediate step, providing more efficient internal reasoning within the model’s “own language" (Hao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2026). However, today’s latent reasoners remain largely sealed behind the model boundary. Unlike decoded text, continuous latent vectors (i) lack native pathways for tool invocation across multi-turn agentic reasoning (Chang et al., 2026), and (ii) do not readily expose human-interpretable semantics, leaving them difficult to supervise during training (Chen et al., 2026) and to audit or debug at inference (Korbak et al., 2025). These constraints keep latent reasoning models from operating as capable agents in their own right.

Taken together, agentic interaction and efficient inner reasoning have so far required a different medium each, leaving the two lines of work apart in the development of next-generation agents. We believe this division can be closed by building a new type of agent that combines both strengths to think beyond text while still acting through it. We call this unified design HybridAgent, one that dynamically navigates between latent reasoning and text-based interaction within a single generation.

Building such an agent is hard, since it needs to handle both dense continuous vectors and sparse discrete tokens as hybrid inputs, and determine when to transition between text and latent modes to balance agentic actions and reasoning efficiency. To offset the hardness, we first revisit the model architecture and extend its autoregressive generation interface to support hybrid inputs. At the heart of this design is HybridLink, a lightweight residual adapter that bridges latent thoughts from the last-layer hidden space back into the input embedding space and enables sequence-wise recurrence within latent mode. Then, we realize multi-turn hybrid generation through the agent’s own working memory, carrying complete hybrid trajectories of text, latent thoughts, and tool observations across turns. Surprisingly, we find that HybridAgent can render its thoughts in latent mode as human-readable pseudo-text, making latent reasoning transparent and directly inspectable rather than opaque.

To further unlock the potential of hybrid reasoning, we equip HybridAgent with dedicated post-training algorithms. HybridSFT first stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation through activation and self-conditioned training, which adapts the backbone to reason over latent thoughts produced by its own HybridLink, enabling reliable coordination between the two components and closing the train-inference mismatch. Then, HybridRL scales agentic reasoning capabilities by training HybridAgent to adaptively balance latent reasoning and text-based interaction. To realize this, we enable policy optimization over hybrid trajectories through hybrid policy factorization and exact rollout replay.

We provide theoretical grounding for HybridAgent through complementary analyses of multi-turn context continuation and hybrid policy optimization. From an architectural standpoint, we show that continuous working memory losslessly preserves the entire hybrid context across different turns. From a learning perspective, the hybrid policy factorization and exact latent-context replay in HybridRL provide a well-founded basis for policy updates over complete hybrid trajectories.

Empirically, we evaluate HybridAgent on 11 benchmarks spanning mathematics, science, medicine, knowledge-intensive search, and challenging agentic reasoning. We instantiate and train HybridAgent with Qwen3-Base models (Yang et al., 2025a) across 4B, 8B, and 14B scales. Compared with frontier LLM agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent reasoning, HybridAgent achieves an average performance improvement of 10.4% and exhibits strong test-time scalability. In terms of efficiency, HybridAgent reduces token usage by 35.5%–54.7%, delivers 1.8×\times–2.6×\times inference speedup, and lowers computational cost by 2.7×\times–3.7×\times. Additional in-depth analyses of training dynamics, reasoning auditability, and agentic tool-use reliability reveal a clear division of labor between the two reasoning modes: HybridAgent shifts more internal reasoning into semantically rich and interpretable latent thoughts, while reserving text for external inspection and tool interaction.

To enable hybrid generation, the agent operates autoregressively in two modes: (i) text, which performs explicit generation in the token space, and (ii) latent, which performs implicit generation in the continuous representation space. Formally, given an input context xx with corresponding input embeddings E=[e1,…,et]∈ℝt×dhE=[e_{1},\dots,e_{t}]\in\mathbb{R}^{t\times d_{h}}, the agent computes the last-layer hidden state hth_{t} through a forward pass, and the hybrid input representation for the next step t+1t+1 is:

3 Building a Hybrid Reasoning Agent

We introduce HybridAgent, a hybrid framework that dynamically navigates between explicit text and continuous latent reasoning within a single unified generation process. As illustrated in Figure 1, the architecture preserves an LLM agent’s autoregressive generation and tool-calling interfaces while accommodating both text and latent inputs. Below, we first present the hybrid interface for seamless text-latent mode transition (Section 3.1), followed by multi-turn hybrid generation (Section 3.2).

3.1 Hybrid Mode Interface

Existing latent reasoning models typically feed the last-layer hidden state hth_{t} directly back as the next-step input et+1e_{t+1}. This design is not well suited to hybrid generation, as substituting hth_{t} for a token embedding creates a representation mismatch with the pretrained input space, making transitions between continuous latent states and discrete tokens difficult. To support both latent and text modes in a shared input interface, we add a lightweight adapter HybridLink to work alongside the backbone.

HybridLink as a Bridge. An LLM agent’s last-layer hidden states naturally encode the semantics of its current generation, so the HybridLink ℛ\mathcal{R} is designed to carry this information from the hidden representation space back into the input embedding space. Formally, given any last-layer hidden state hth_{t}, HybridLink simulates its corresponding next-step input embedding as:

et+1=ℛ⁡(ht)=ht+W2​σ​(W1​ht),\displaystyle e_{t+1}=\mathcal{R}(h_{t})=h_{t}+W_{2}\,\sigma\!\left(W_{1}h_{t}\right), (4)

where W1,W2W_{1},W_{2} are standard linear projections, σ\sigma is an activation function (e.g., GELU). As the residual connection largely preserves the original semantics of hth_{t}, HybridLink only needs to align the distributional difference rather than learn the entire projection from scratch. Accordingly, the link module is lightweight, with approximately 2​dh22d_{h}^{2} parameters (e.g., ∼\sim10M parameters for a 4B LLM).

Dynamic Text-Latent Mode Transition. Next, we describe how HybridAgent transitions between text and latent modes during generation, together with the entry and exit decisions for each mode.

In text mode, HybridAgent behaves exactly as a standard LLM, sampling the next token from the vocabulary at each step. The process continues until the agent generates one special token <latent>, which serves as the entry anchor for the latent mode. For the next forward pass, the agent uses HybridLink for latent reasoning in place of the LM head and token embedding layer.

In latent mode, each step’s last-layer hidden state is passed through HybridLink via Eq. 4, allowing HybridAgent to continue its generation flow entirely in latent space without token decoding and re-embedding. This sequence-wise recurrent computation over continuous representations extends the agent’s effective reasoning depth, enabling more expressive internal reasoning. The latent reasoning span terminates when the semantics of the last-layer hidden state hth_{t} align with the exit anchor </latent>. Specifically, at any latent step tt, the latent mode closes by satisfying the condition:

arg​maxv∈𝒱cos(ℛ(ht),Emb(v))=</latent>.\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\;\cos\bigl(\mathcal{R}(h_{t}),\,\operatorname{Emb}(v)\bigr)=\texttt{</latent>}. (5)

HybridAgent then returns to its text mode, and this transition continues during generation. At each step, the agent adaptively decides whether to remain in its current mode or switch, allowing the length and frequency of text and latent spans to emerge dynamically rather than follow preset configurations.

Interpretable Latent Mode. During hybrid generation, a useful property of HybridAgent is that its latent mode remains decoding-free yet directly interpretable. To inspect any latent reasoning span, one can easily recover its semantics by mapping each latent step produced by HybridLink to its nearest token embedding, as in Eq. 5. We illustrate this interpretability property clearly in Figure 2.

3.2 Multi-Turn Hybrid Generation over Working Memory

In standard LLM agents, each turn’s generated content and tool outputs are appended to the textual context and re-encoded as the next turn’s input prefix. Hybrid trajectories, however, interleave text tokens with latent vectors and can’t be reconstructed through conventional tokenization alone. Instead, HybridAgent carries the complete context across turns through its continuous working memory.

Cross-Turn Working Memory. Recall that a single-turn hybrid trajectory τ\tau in Eq. 3 consists of model-generated text, latent thoughts, and external tool interactions. During input construction, all contents are mapped into the same input space through either the input embedding layer or HybridLink. This shared space allows the Transformer to process all three components uniformly and collect their KV entries throughout generation. We leverage these accumulated KV entries as the HybridAgent’s continuous working memory to achieve multi-turn hybrid generation.

As illustrated in Figure 3, HybridAgent first initializes its working memory ℳ\mathcal{M} from the input context xx and then accumulates the KV entries generated throughout the first-turn trajectory τ(1)\tau^{(1)}, i.e.,

ℳ(0)\displaystyle\mathcal{M}^{(0)} =[K≤|x|,V≤|x|],\displaystyle=\bigl[K_{\leq|x|},\,V_{\leq|x|}\bigr], (6)
ℳ(1)\displaystyle\mathcal{M}^{(1)} =ℳ(0)⊕[K≤t,V≤t],t=1,…,|τ(1)|.\displaystyle=\mathcal{M}^{(0)}\oplus\bigl[K_{\leq t},V_{\leq t}\bigr],\quad t=1,\dots,|\tau^{(1)}|.

Here, ℳ(1)\mathcal{M}^{(1)} preserves the complete first-turn hybrid context in positional order across all Transformer layers. For each subsequent turn, the agent directly resumes generation from the current working memory and updates it by appending newly generated KV entries at each step. This process continues across the sequence of hybrid trajectories {τ(1),τ(2),…,τ(n)}\{\tau^{(1)},\tau^{(2)},\dots,\tau^{(n)}\} until the final answer is produced. We further provide a formal justification for this continuation process in Appendix A. Overall, multi-turn hybrid generation proceeds over one continuous working memory flow, preserving the complete hybrid context across turns without requiring intermediate token-space reconstruction.

4 Learning to Perform Hybrid Reasoning

With the overall framework in place, we now turn to training. As HybridAgent leaves the backbone architecture intact, no pre-training from scratch is required. Instead, we adapt the standard agentic post-training pipeline of supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning to the hybrid setting. The two training stages serve complementary roles: SFT teaches the agent to coordinate with HybridLink and instantiate reliable tool use for stable hybrid generation (Section 4.1), while RL further scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text (Section 4.2).

4.1 Stabilize Generation via Hybrid Supervised Fine-tuning

As a first step toward stabilizing hybrid reasoning in HybridAgent, we design the entire HybridSFT stage through a hybrid data curation pipeline and a staged training procedure.

Hybrid Data Recipe. To curate high-quality training data, we filter existing text-based agentic SFT datasets from multiple sources and convert them into hybrid trajectories through automatic annotation. We assign reasoning steps to latent mode based on both LLM Experts’ judgments and target models’ own prediction entropy, while retaining a small set of key steps for tool interactions and external debugging/auditing in text mode (see Appendix E for data curation details).

Format and HybridLink Activation. As a warm start, we adapt the backbone to the hybrid data format and initialize the HybridLink. For format activation, we perform standard text SFT to teach the backbone when to enter and exit latent mode by emitting the two special anchor tokens. We then freeze the backbone and train HybridLink to align last-layer hidden states at latent positions with their target input embeddings. For a training instance (x,y)∈𝒟SFT(x,y)\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{SFT}}, the activation objectives are:

ℒBackbone=CE⁡(fθ​(x),y),\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{Backbone}}=\mathrm{CE}\bigl(f_{\theta}(x),\,y\bigr), (7)
ℒHybridLink =λcos(1−cos(ℛ(hlat),Emb(ylat)))+λmse∥ℛ(hlat)−Emb(ylat)∥22,\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{HybridLink }}=\lambda_{\cos}\Bigl(1-\cos\bigl(\mathcal{R}(h_{\text{lat}}),\,\operatorname{Emb}(y_{\text{lat}})\bigr)\Bigr)+\lambda_{\mathrm{mse}}\bigl\lVert\mathcal{R}(h_{\text{lat}})-\operatorname{Emb}(y_{\text{lat}})\bigr\rVert_{2}^{2},

where hlath_{\mathrm{lat}} is the last-layer hidden states at latent positions, ylaty_{\mathrm{lat}} is the corresponding ground-truth text tokens, and λcos,λmse\lambda_{\cos},\lambda_{\mathrm{mse}} balance directional and magnitude alignment, respectively.

Self-Conditioned HybridSFT. The activation provides a well-aligned initialization, but the backbone has not yet learned to reason over latent thoughts produced by its own HybridLink (see Appendix B.1 for details on this train-inference mismatch). We therefore adopt a two-pass self-conditioned training scheme as illustrated in Figure 4. In the first pass, HybridAgent is teacher-forced on the ground-truth hybrid sequence. HybridLink maps the generated last-layer hidden states at latent positions one step ahead to form latent inputs for the next pass. In the second pass, HybridAgent processes the same sequence but replaces the ground-truth latent embeddings with its own latent inputs. We jointly supervise text and latent positions on the second pass as:

ℒHybridSFT=ℒBackbone+ℒHybridLink ,\mathcal{L}_{\text{HybridSFT}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{Backbone}}+\mathcal{L}_{\text{HybridLink }}, (8)

where the CE loss ℒBackbone\mathcal{L}_{\text{Backbone}} and regression loss ℒHybridLink \mathcal{L}_{\text{HybridLink }} are applied only at text and latent positions, respectively. Overall, HybridSFT trains the agent to coordinate its backbone with HybridLink for coherent reasoning across text and latent modes, supporting stable hybrid generation at inference.

4.2 Scale Reasoning via Hybrid Reinforcement Learning

A HybridAgent cannot straightforwardly adopt popular RL algorithms such as PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) or GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), as they assume every generated position carries a token-level likelihood. Specifically, at each position tt, standard RL computes the per-token importance ratio as:

ρt=πθ​(yt∣y<t)πθold​(yt∣y<t),\displaystyle\rho_{t}=\frac{\pi_{\theta}\bigl(y_{t}\mid y_{<t}\bigr)}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}\bigl(y_{t}\mid y_{<t}\bigr)}, (9)

where πθ,πθold\pi_{\theta},\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}} denote the current and rollout policies. At latent positions, however, HybridAgent generates continuous vectors rather than sampled tokens, leaving no token-level likelihood. Thus, the importance ratio ρt\rho_{t} is undefined. We address this incompatibility with two simple components.

Hybrid Policy Factorization. Recall that, in a hybrid trajectory, latent thoughts are computed entirely in the continuous latent space through HybridLink, and tool responses are the masked observations from the environment. Thus, policy sampling during rollout is confined to model-generated text positions. To justify why policy optimization needs only to operate over these sampled positions, we formalize the hybrid policy factorization below with detailed theoretical analyses.

Proposition 4.1 (Hybrid Policy Factorization).

Let τ\tau be a hybrid trajectory generated by the policy πθ\pi_{\theta} (induced by fθf_{\theta}) with fixed HybridLink ℛ\mathcal{R}. Then the hybrid policy factorizes as:

πθ​(τ∣x)=∏t∈𝒯πθ​(yt∣x,τ<t),\displaystyle\pi_{\theta}(\tau\mid x)\;=\;\prod_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\pi_{\theta}\bigl(y_{t}\mid x,\,\tau_{<t}\bigr), (10)

where 𝒯\mathcal{T} is the set of sampled text positions of trajectory τ\tau.

The proof and additional theoretical justifications are provided in Appendix C. Proposition 4.1 shows that likelihood-ratio updates over sampled text positions are sufficient to optimize the full hybrid trajectory, making the importance ratio in Eq. 9 well-defined for the HybridAgent policy.

Policy Update via Exact Rollout Replay. Policy optimization generally involves rebuilding a differentiable computation graph for the rollouts. Applying this to HybridAgent further requires recomputing sampled text-token likelihoods conditioned on the same preceding latent thoughts used during rollout. We satisfy this requirement via exact latent-context replay. During hybrid rollout, we record latent thoughts alongside sampled text tokens and tool observations. During policy updates, we replay the full hybrid trajectory in embedding space with a single differentiable forward pass, keeping the recorded latent inputs unchanged while recomputing the sampled likelihoods in Eq. 10.

Algorithm 1 outlines the full HybridRL training procedure. We keep the HybridLink fixed to preserve deterministic latent transitions. For the reward design, we simply formulate it as:

r⁡(τ)=rcorrect+rformat+rtool,r(\tau)=r_{\mathrm{correct}}+r_{\mathrm{format}}+r_{\mathrm{tool}}, (11)

where rcorrectr_{\mathrm{correct}} measures answer correctness, rformatr_{\mathrm{format}} penalizes invalid formatting, and rtoolr_{\mathrm{tool}} encourages multi-tool use. We impose no explicit reward for mode usage, allowing HybridAgent to adaptively balance text and latent generation and discover effective hybrid reasoning strategies during RL.

5 Empirical Evaluations

Tasks and Datasets. We conduct comprehensive evaluations of HybridAgent on 11 benchmarks across various domains: (i) Mathematical Reasoning, including AIME 25 (math-ai, 2025), AIME 26 (MathArena, 2026), and MATH500 (HuggingFaceH4, 2023); (ii) Knowledge-Intensive Reasoning, including GPQA-Diamond (Rein et al., 2023), MedQA (Yang et al., 2024), and MuSiQue (Trivedi et al., 2022); and (iii) Agentic Reasoning, including General AI Assistants (GAIA) (Mialon et al., 2024), Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE) (Center for AI Safety et al., 2026), WebWalker (Wu et al., 2025), SealQA (Pham et al., 2026), and DeepSearchQA (DSQA) (Gupta et al., 2026). We adopt the standard evaluation metric for each dataset. Additional benchmark details are in Appendix H.1.

Baselines. For baseline comparisons, we evaluate HybridAgent against (i) Text-based Agentic Methods, covering standard text SFT (with tools) and multi-turn tool-integrated RL methods such as GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) and ARPO (Dong et al., 2025b); (ii) Latent Reasoning Methods, including SoftThinking (Zhang et al., 2025), Coconut (Hao et al., 2024), and SoftCoT (Xu et al., 2025b); (iii) Frontier LLM Agents, including GPT-5.6-Luna (OpenAI, 2026), Kimi-K3 (Team, 2026), GLM-5.3-Flash (GLM-5-Team and others, 2026), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026), QwQ-32B (Team, 2025); and (iv) Agentic Frameworks, including ReAct (Yao et al., 2023), Search-o1 (Li et al., 2025a), and WebThinker (Li et al., 2025b). Additional baseline details are provided in Appendix H.2.

Models and Training Setups. We instantiate HybridAgent with Qwen3-Base backbones (Yang et al., 2025a) at three scales of 4B, 8B, and 14B. We then apply HybridSFT with 54K hybrid trajectories curated through our automatic annotation pipeline, followed by HybridRL with 12K deep reasoning examples (Yu et al., 2025) and 1K agentic search examples (Dong et al., 2025b). During RL, we set rollout batches of 512 trajectories (64×864\times 8), followed by one optimization pass over 8 minibatches.

Implementation Details. HybridAgent interacts with external environments primarily through two types of tools: a Python interpreter within sandbox environments and a live search engine (e.g., Tavily). We cap tool usage at 10 calls per trajectory and retrieve the top 10 snippets for each search query. As current serving engines do not support multi-turn hybrid generation, we extend the training and inference infrastructure to enable text, latent, and tool-calling transitions and persistent KV working-memory transfer. RL rollouts use a sampling temperature of 1.0, and evaluation uses temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, and top-k 20. We conduct experiments on H100 GPUs using five independent seeds. Additional training/inference details and hyperparameter setups are provided in Appendix H.3.

5.1 Scaling Performance via Hybrid Reasoning

Main Results. Tables 1 and 2 report the overall performance of HybridAgent across 11 benchmarks spanning math, science, medicine, and knowledge search domains. On challenging agentic reasoning benchmarks, HybridAgent delivers competitive performance over larger frontier LLM agents and specialized tool-use frameworks, with HybridAgent (14B) improving over the strongest agentic baseline by an average of 17.4%. In addition, under matched model sizes and training budgets, HybridSFT and HybridRL demonstrate consistent training effectiveness and improve over corresponding text/latent baselines by 18.5% at the SFT stage and 10.4% at the RL stage. Together, HybridAgent combines the strengths of text-based agentic tool use with faster and more expressive latent reasoning, allowing the agent to interact externally while achieving deeper thinking depth internally.

Scaling Hybrid Reasoning at Test Time. To further examine the test-time scalability of our hybrid reasoning paradigm, we increase inference compute budgets through additional sampling and evaluate pass@k performance. Figure 5 shows that HybridAgent exhibits a clear upward trend as sampling increases across all model scales, while benefiting more from increased test-time compute than agents with text-only RL. Additional 4B-scale experiments and case studies are in Appendix G and J.

5.2 Efficiency Advantage on Hybrid Generation

Beyond performance effectiveness, a key architectural advantage of HybridAgent is that latent mode enables efficient generation without costly explicit token decoding. We evaluate this property empirically along three complementary dimensions: (i) token throughput, (ii) wall-clock inference time, and (iii) actual computation cost. As shown in Figures 6 and 7, HybridAgent adaptively balances its hybrid reasoning across text and latent modes by using 2.7×2.7\times fewer text tokens, reducing total generation steps by up to 54%, and achieving 2.1×2.1\times faster inference than text-based baselines. Together with the cost analyses in Table 9 (see Appendix G.2), HybridAgent generates more concise and refined reasoning trajectories, reducing inference overhead and cost.

6 In-depth Analyses

RoadMap. We further analyze HybridAgent from 3 complementary perspectives to assess the method design and better understand its hybrid reasoning behavior. (i) Training Dynamics: We study how self-conditioning in HybridSFT improves reasoning performance (Table 8) and latent interpretability (Figure 8), and how HybridRL shifts more reasoning into latent mode while strengthening tool interaction (Figure 9). (ii) Latent-Mode: We intervene on latent content, ordering, and reasoning depth to examine HybridAgent’s causal reliance on latent thoughts (Table 5), and ablate HybridLink architectures to assess the benefits of residual alignment (Table 6). (iii) Text-Mode: We evaluate text-based agentic tool use (Figure 10) and auditability of HybridAgent (Table 7) to verify that text-mode supports reliable environment interaction and remains informative for external monitoring/debugging.

6.1 Training Dynamics on HybridSFT and HybridRL

Self-Conditioning Enables Effective and Interpretable HybridSFT. To understand why self-conditioned training is necessary for HybridAgent during SFT, we compare HybridSFT against variants with only format and HybridLink activations as well as latent SFT baselines like Coconut, from both performance and interpretability perspectives. As shown in Table 8, although all SFT variants improve the original shared Qwen3-14B-Base backbone, activation alone remains insufficient. Self-conditioned supervision further improves performance by an average of 30.5% over HybridLink activation, bringing HybridSFT to parity with standard text SFT across all three math benchmarks.

We further probe the semantics of the latent thoughts produced by each method over 200 questions spanning all downstream domains. Figure 8 reveals a clear progression, where HybridLink activation first makes latent contents more interpretable, and the additional self-conditioned training sharpens the latent readability and semantic informativeness. We then take a closer look to examine individual test instances through detailed case studies in Appendix J. Specifically, methods with low faithfulness and specificity generally produce largely unreadable artifacts of the embedding geometry, whereas the complete HybridSFT yields clear and semantically coherent latent readouts. Overall, these analyses reveal that self-conditioned training is essential to HybridSFT for making the latent reasoning traces in HybridAgent fully transparent and directly interpretable.

Training Dynamics of HybridRL. We analyze HybridAgent’s training behaviors to examine how it dynamically shifts and allocates reasoning effort across text/latent modes under HybridRL. In Figure 9, as the training step increases, our 14B agent progressively allocates more generation to latent mode while simultaneously strengthening its tool-invocation capability. Through training, HybridAgent adaptively learns to better utilize its two modes, shifting more reasoning into faster latent thinking while selectively exposing only key steps for external auditing and tool use through the text interface.

Reward Shaping in HybridRL. We ablate each reward component in Eq. 11 using HybridAgent (8B), removing one term at a time under otherwise identical setups. In Table 4, all three components provide complementary supervision. Excluding rcorrectr_{\text{correct}} causes the largest overall degradation, reducing performance by 6.4%-17.8%, while removing rformatr_{\text{format}} consistently lowers performance by 4.7%-6.9%. The benefit of rtoolr_{\text{tool}} is most pronounced on agentic benchmarks such as GAIA and WebWalker. Since the reward is granted only to trajectories that invoke both Python and search tools, removing rtoolr_{\text{tool}} has a minor effect on MATH500, where Python alone is typically sufficient, but reduces GAIA and WebWalker by 11.2% and 3.5%. Overall, each reward component provides complementary supervision for answer correctness, format structure, and effective multi-tool use.

6.2 Causal Reliance and HybridLink Design in Latent Mode

Does HybridAgent Causally Rely on its Latent Mode Thoughts? To examine whether latent thoughts are functionally used during hybrid reasoning, we intervene on the latent vectors generated by 8B and 14B HybridAgent on the MATH500 downstream task. We perturb their content, ordering, and reasoning duration through 4 different types of controlled interventions, including (i) noise perturbation, (ii) latent replacement, (iii) latent permutation, and (iv) latent computation restriction. Table 5 details the intervention setups and reports performance under each scenario.

As shown in the table, disrupting latent thoughts consistently degrades performance across both scales. Specifically, cross-problem and random-token replacement reduce accuracy by 44.9-47.0% and 49.4-51.3%, while disrupting their ordering or restricting each latent span to one step leads to 13.4-15.0% degradation. Notably, cross-problem replacement causes substantially greater degradation than even stronger Gaussian perturbations, suggesting that performance depends on the semantic content of latent thoughts rather than perturbation magnitude alone. These analysis results on causal interventions indicate that HybridAgent functionally relies on the semantics, ordering, and sufficient reasoning depth of its latent thoughts during hybrid reasoning.

HybridLink Design. We next validate the effectiveness of HybridLink and its residual connection by comparing our adopted 2-layer residual design against 4 alternative architectures: (i) direct hidden-state reuse (i.e., et+1e_{t+1}==hth_{t}) without learned alignment, (ii) 1-layer projection, (iii) 1-layer projection with residual connection, and (iv) 2-layer projection without residual connection. We end-to-end train each HybridLink variant with the 14B backbone under the same setup and evaluate across tasks.

As shown in Table 6, the full two-layer residual design of HybridLink yields consistent gains across all three downstream benchmarks, with the residual branch benefiting both one- and two-layer projection networks. Specifically, incorporating the residual connection contributes an average improvement of 4.3% across different layer depths. This observed trend aligns with our design motivation in Section 3.1, where the residual connection preserves the semantics of input last-layer hidden states while the learned projection aligns these representations with the input embedding space. Together, these two components make HybridLink a more effective and stable interface for hybrid training and generation.

6.3 Tool Use and Reasoning Auditability in Text Mode

Does HybridAgent Text-Mode Preserve Agentic Tool Use? In Figure 10, we analyze agentic tool-calling capabilities by comparing HybridAgent with normal LLM agents trained on GRPO, examining whether hybrid reasoning preserves reliable external interactions through its text mode. Across 8B and 14B scales, HybridAgent achieves higher valid tool-call rates while matching the 99.7% execution success of valid calls, showing that hybrid reasoning preserves a reliable text-mode tool interface. More importantly, the gains extend beyond call validity, as HybridAgent improves final-answer accuracy by 2.2%-44.1% on questions where tools are invoked. The 4.5%-7.7% higher useful tool-call rate further indicates that HybridAgent not only invokes tools correctly, but also retrieves evidence that more directly contributes to solving the task. These findings suggest that HybridAgent preserves the reliable and effective agentic tool use of standard LLM agents through its text mode, while exposing fewer text tokens with interleaved latent reasoning.

Does HybridAgent Text-Mode Preserve External Auditability? A natural question of hybrid reasoning is whether shifting computation into latent mode might potentially compromise the external auditability provided by text. To examine this, we evaluate HybridAgent against matched text agents on MATH500 and AIME25/26, covering 560 problems under identical setups. For each question, an external observer sees only the exposed text steps, tool calls, and tool outputs, while latent spans remain hidden behind their boundary markers. We evaluate four complementary dimensions following commonly adopted evaluation protocols.

  • •

    Monitoring: Measure whether a blind external monitor can predict rollout correctness from the input problem and visible trace generated by each agent, following Baker et al. (2025). We report AUROC using GPT-4o-mini (Hurst et al., 2024) as a weak monitor, which relies primarily on the visible trace rather than solving the problem independently, and GPT-5.6-Luna (OpenAI, 2026) as a strong monitor with more powerful task-solving capability.

  • •

    Debugging: Following first-error localization (Zheng et al., 2025a), a judge model (GPT-5.6-Luna) is deployed to identify the first erroneous visible step from a failed rollout and produces a corrective hint, with the diagnosis verified against the reference ground-truth solution.

  • •

    Correction: Each failed problem is re-attempted using the corrective hint generated during debugging, and compared against a generic correctness-only feedback baseline (Huang et al., 2024) that simply tells the agent its previous answer was incorrect and asks it to retry.

  • •

    Rationale Sufficiency: Following sufficiency evaluation in DeYoung et al. (2020), a weak reader (GPT-4o-mini) predicts the agent’s own answer from the exposed text steps alone after removing the final answer, measuring whether the visible trace retains sufficient decision-relevant information.

As shown in Table 7, HybridAgent exposes 43%-49% fewer text-mode tokens while performing 170-183 reasoning steps in latent mode, yet the visible trace contains 26%-28% more key reasoning steps per 100 tokens. This reduction preserves external monitorability, with AUROC remaining within 0.022 of matched text agents across both weak and strong monitors. The exposed text also remains debuggable, localizing the first error in 98%-99% of failed rollouts and yielding reference-consistent diagnoses in 97%-98% of cases with below 1% answer leakage. Moreover, text-derived corrective hints produce significant fix-rate gains of 5.4 and 9.1 points at 14B and 8B, while rationale sufficiency remains comparable to or higher than text agents. As shown by the analyses above, HybridAgent uses its text mode to maintain a compact yet informative textual interface for external monitoring, debugging, and correction. This provides an important safeguard for agent generation, facilitating human auditing and intervention while preserving efficient internal reasoning.

7 Related Work

Latent Reasoning Beyond Text. Recent works have explored applying intermediate reasoning beyond discrete language tokens into continuous hidden spaces (Hao et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025a; Yu et al., 2026), allowing models to perform internal computation without explicitly verbalizing every reasoning step (Geiping et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2025b). Existing approaches broadly realize this idea by inputting last-layer hidden states (Saunshi et al., 2025; Tack et al., 2026), compressing textual chains of thought into latent representations (Cheng and Van Durme, 2024; Zhang et al., 2026a), or directly optimizing continuous reasoning trajectories (Tan et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2024). These methods improve reasoning efficiency and depth but make direct inspection and external interaction difficult (Korbak et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026). HybridAgent builds on this direction by integrating directly inspectable latent reasoning as a native built-in mode within the agentic generation process, while preserving direct text-based auditing and tool interaction.

Agentic Reasoning and Tool Use. Frontier LLM agents (Team, 2026; GLM-5-Team and others, 2026; DeepSeek-AI, 2026) extend reasoning beyond static generation by interacting with external environments through tools (Shen, 2024; Qu et al., 2025), such as search engines (Jin et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025b), code interpreters (Feng et al., 2026; Bianchi et al., 2026), and APIs (Qin et al., 2024; Patil et al., 2025). A growing line of work further improves these capabilities through post-training over multi-turn tool-use trajectories (Dong et al., 2025a; Qian et al., 2025), enabling agents to plan, act, observe, and revise their reasoning (Su et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025c). Despite this progress, existing agentic frameworks remain text-centric for both model-side reasoning and environment-side interaction, incurring large generation overhead from verbalizing every intermediate step (Cuadron et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025a). HybridAgent decouples these roles by interleaving continuous thoughts for internal reasoning and retaining text only where explicit interaction and monitoring are required.

We discuss additional related work and its relation to HybridAgent in Appendix D.

8 Discussion and Future Directions

Implications for Frontier Agent Safety and Secure Deployment. Frontier labs (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic) provide API-based access to reasoning models while hiding the chain-of-thought from customers to protect intellectual property and limit information leakage, yet Panfilov et al. (2026) show that the encrypted traces returned to clients can be replayed into a sibling model and transcribed verbatim. HybridAgent places proprietary reasoning on a different footing. Latent thoughts exist only as backbone hidden states that are readable solely through the provider-owned HybridLink (Section 3), so no text exists to leak. The same property aids monitoring. Because the latent trace is held by the provider rather than the client, providers can assess the safety of reasoning and actions over the full readout, including the portion users never see, while the agent benefits from faster inner thinking. Text mode is then reserved for what users legitimately need, such as tool calls, key decisions, and the final answer, preserving an auditable trace without exposing the full reasoning.

Future Directions on Hybrid Agent Harness and Efficient Post-Training. Future work can build a new type of agent harness around HybridAgent, where latent working memory is a first-class component. Context management can then operate on KV entries directly, workflows can schedule steps by mode, keeping tool calls and human-facing checkpoints in text while routine computation stays latent, and one agent’s hybrid trajectory can serve as its message to another. Hybrid generation can also make post-training more efficient. Because latent thoughts remain auditable during rollout, an external critic can assign step-level credit to latent spans, branch promising trajectories, or terminate ones whose latent reasoning has already gone wrong, before any text or tool call is produced.

9 Conclusion

We introduce HybridAgent, a unified hybrid reasoning framework that combines efficient latent reasoning with text-based inspection and tool interaction. HybridAgent enables multi-turn hybrid generation through both architectural designs and dedicated post-training algorithms on SFT and RL stages. Across 11 benchmarks and 3 model scales, HybridAgent achieves strong performance against advanced LLM agents and agentic frameworks spanning text-based and latent reasoning methods, while substantially reducing inference time, token usage, and computational cost. Overall, HybridAgent provides a scalable and efficient framework for next-generation agents that can reason beyond human language while retaining agentic interaction in environments and external inspectability.

Appendix A Multi-turn Continuation over Working Memory

Following our notation in Section 2, denote the input sequence E≤t=[e1,…,et]E_{\leq t}=[e_{1},\ldots,e_{t}] and working memory ℳt=[K≤t,V≤t]\mathcal{M}_{t}=[K_{\leq t},V_{\leq t}] at step tt, where KK and VV collect the keys and values across all layers.

Theorem A.1 (Lossless Multi-Turn Working Memory).

Given the multi-turn generation process in Section 3.2, consider the fixed HybridAgent fθf_{\theta} and HybridLink ℛ\mathcal{R} under consistent inference settings. At step tt, let ht+1h_{t+1} be the hidden output obtained by processing et+1e_{t+1} with the complete working memory ℳt\mathcal{M}_{t}. Then,

ht+1⏟process ​et+1​ using ​ℳt=fθ​([E≤t;et+1])⏟apply the complete hybrid prefix.\underbrace{h_{t+1}}_{\text{process }e_{t+1}\text{ using }\mathcal{M}_{t}}=\underbrace{f_{\theta}([E_{\leq t};e_{t+1}])}_{\text{apply the complete hybrid prefix}}. (12)

Thus, working memory preserves the text, latent, and tool observations for continued reasoning, without converting latent thoughts into text.

Remark A.2.

Theorem A.1 shows that retaining complete working memory preserves the effect of the full hybrid history on subsequent generation across turns. This justifies resuming HybridAgent after tool interactions without reconstructing earlier turns or converting latent thoughts into text.

Proof.

Fix fθf_{\theta} and HybridLink ℛ\mathcal{R}, and use the same deterministic causal operations, masks, and positional encoding, preserving all existing KV entries. Each cached forward run produces both a hidden output and an updated memory:

(et+1,ℳt)⏟next input and preceding context→cached forward run(ht+1,ℳt+1)⏟hidden output and updated memory.\underbrace{(e_{t+1},\mathcal{M}_{t})}_{\text{next input and preceding context}}\xrightarrow{\text{cached forward run}}\underbrace{(h_{t+1},\mathcal{M}_{t+1})}_{\text{hidden output and updated memory}}.

The hidden output determines the next text distribution or latent input, while the updated memory provides the context for the following forward run. Here, layer and head indices are omitted for notation simplicity. We compare a memory-based forward run with a full-prefix forward run under the same model and inference settings.

Base case (t=1t=1). Both forward runs start with empty memory and the same input e1e_{1}. At the first layer, they produce the same queries, keys, values, and attention outputs. The remaining token-wise operations produce the same input to the next layer. Repeating this argument through all layers gives

ℳ1=[K1,V1].\mathcal{M}_{1}=[K_{1},V_{1}].

Both forward runs also produce the same final hidden output, h1=fθ​([e1])h_{1}=f_{\theta}([e_{1}]).

Induction hypothesis. Suppose that, after processing step tt, the stored keys and values are equal to those computed by a full-prefix forward run:

ℳt⏟stored KV memory=[K≤t,V≤t]⏟KV computed from the complete prefix ​E≤t.\underbrace{\mathcal{M}_{t}}_{\text{stored KV memory}}=\underbrace{[K_{\leq t},V_{\leq t}]}_{\text{KV computed from the complete prefix }E_{\leq t}}.

Induction step (t→t+1t\to t+1). Causality and unchanged positional encoding preserve the earlier keys and values when et+1e_{t+1} is appended. Both forward runs start the first layer with the same input et+1e_{t+1}.

If their inputs to the current layer are equal, each head computes the same query, new keys and values. The earlier KV entries are equal by the induction hypothesis. With the same attention mask, each head therefore produces the same attention output. The remaining token-wise operations produce the same input to the following layer.

Repeating this implication through all layers gives the same final hidden output:

ht+1=fθ​([E≤t;et+1]).h_{t+1}=f_{\theta}([E_{\leq t};e_{t+1}]).

It also gives the same new keys and values, Kt+1,Vt+1K_{t+1},V_{t+1}. Appending them to the stored memory and substituting the induction hypothesis yields

ℳt+1\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{t+1} =ℳt⊕[Kt+1,Vt+1]\displaystyle=\mathcal{M}_{t}\oplus[K_{t+1},V_{t+1}]
=[K≤t,V≤t]⊕[Kt+1,Vt+1]\displaystyle=[K_{\leq t},V_{\leq t}]\oplus[K_{t+1},V_{t+1}]
=[K≤t+1,V≤t+1].\displaystyle=[K_{\leq t+1},V_{\leq t+1}].

Thus, the updated memory satisfies the induction hypothesis at t+1t+1, while the hidden-output equality establishes Eq. 12. By induction, at every input position, the cached forward run produces the same hidden output and updated KV memory as the full-prefix forward run.

At the end of each turn j∈{1,…,n}j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, let t=|x|+∑i=1j|τ(i)|t=|x|+\sum_{i=1}^{j}|\tau^{(i)}| count all input slots processed so far, including the initial context and all text, latent, and tool-observation inputs. Starting from ℳ(0)=[K≤|x|,V≤|x|]\mathcal{M}^{(0)}=[K_{\leq|x|},V_{\leq|x|}], repeated concatenation gives

ℳ(j)\displaystyle\mathcal{M}^{(j)} =ℳ(0)⊕[K|x|+1:t,V|x|+1:t]\displaystyle=\mathcal{M}^{(0)}\oplus[K_{|x|+1:t},V_{|x|+1:t}]
=[K≤|x|,V≤|x|]⊕[K|x|+1:t,V|x|+1:t]\displaystyle=[K_{\leq|x|},V_{\leq|x|}]\oplus[K_{|x|+1:t},V_{|x|+1:t}]
=[K≤t,V≤t].\displaystyle=[K_{\leq t},V_{\leq t}].

Each new entry is appended exactly once, so turn boundaries do not change the memory used by subsequent forward runs.

Finally, the established hidden-state equality gives

Softmax⁡(Wout​ht)\displaystyle\operatorname{Softmax}(W_{\mathrm{out}}h_{t}) =Softmax⁡(Wout​fθ​(E≤t)),\displaystyle=\operatorname{Softmax}(W_{\mathrm{out}}f_{\theta}(E_{\leq t})),
ℛ⁡(ht)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}(h_{t}) =ℛ⁡(fθ​(E≤t)).\displaystyle=\mathcal{R}(f_{\theta}(E_{\leq t})).

where we retain the corresponding hidden states and tool observations, while using the same random draws for sampling and tool execution in both runs. Then, both runs process the same next input with the same memory and reasoning mode, producing the same hidden output and updated KV memory. Repeating this argument step by step gives identical subsequent hybrid sequences under the shared random draws, and hence identical generation probabilities. Therefore, working memory preserves the effect of the complete hybrid history across turns, without reconstructing latent thoughts as text.

∎

Appendix B Design and Analyses of Hybrid Supervised Fine-tuning

We expand on the method description of HybridSFT (Section 4.1), providing additional design justifications and implementation details for the overall training scheme.

B.1 Why Self-Conditioned Training?

The format and HybridLink activation provide a well-aligned initialization, but both are teacher-forced (Figure 11, left). At every latent position, the backbone consumes the ground-truth embedding Emb⁡(y)\mathrm{Emb}(y), and HybridLink is trained only to match its output ℛ⁡(h)\mathcal{R}(h) to that target; the prediction itself is never fed back as an input. At inference, the agent instead runs free (Figure 11, right). Once it enters latent mode, every subsequent input is its own ℛ⁡(h)\mathcal{R}(h), which neither the backbone nor HybridLink has been conditioned on. This train-inference mismatch is akin to exposure bias (Ranzato et al., 2015; Bengio et al., 2015), a standard issue in autoregressive sequence models that are trained on ground-truth prefixes but consume their own predictions at inference.

It is worth noting that exposure bias is present in both text and latent modes, since both feed the model’s own outputs back as inputs. In text mode (as in standard LLM SFT), each fed-back input is sampled and re-embedded, and thus always corresponds to a token in the discrete vocabulary. A prediction error, where the sampled token differs from the ground-truth target, only changes which token is fed back; the input representation itself never leaves the set seen in training, so errors cannot compound in the input space. Latent mode, in contrast, has no such projection. ℛ⁡(h)\mathcal{R}(h) is continuous and fed back unquantized, so even a small deviation from the target embedding becomes an input the backbone has never seen in training. This deviation propagates to the next hidden state and hence the next latent input, compounding over the tens to hundreds of steps in a latent span and gradually eroding the semantic coherence of the latent trace.

Self-conditioned HybridSFT closes this gap by training both components on the model’s own generated latent inputs. As in Figure 4, the teacher-forced first pass applies HybridLink to the last-layer hidden state at each latent position, yielding the model’s own prediction of the next latent input. The second pass then replaces the ground-truth latent embeddings with these predictions and trains the backbone and HybridLink jointly, so both parts learn under the same latent inputs they encounter at inference.

Under this training scheme, the backbone learns to read, and HybridLink learns to produce, latent inputs under the same conditions they encounter at inference. Thus, HybridAgent is trained as an integrated whole rather than two separately activated components.

B.2 Learning When to Enter and Exit Latent Mode

As stated in Section 3, HybridAgent transitions between modes through two special tokens, the entry anchor <latent> and the exit anchor </latent>. Within a latent span, these anchors are the only positions supervised by ℒBackbone\mathcal{L}_{\text{Backbone}}, while every other latent position is supervised by ℒHybridLink \mathcal{L}_{\text{HybridLink }} alone. The two transitions are not symmetric, however. Entering latent mode is decided in text mode, where the backbone samples the next token from the vocabulary as usual, whereas exiting must be decided from a continuous latent state through the readout in Eq. 5. HybridSFT therefore treats the entry anchor as an ordinary token and gives the exit anchor dedicated supervision.

Entry as a Text-Mode Decision. Since entering is a text mode decision, <latent> is simply a cross-entropy target, and the backbone learns from the preceding context when to switch. The anchor position then serves as the first latent step, with its last-layer hidden state passed through HybridLink to produce the next latent input, so the span begins without any additional mechanism.

Exit as a Latent-Mode Decision. Exiting takes place in latent mode, where no token is sampled. By Eq. 5, a span closes when the HybridLink’s output ℛ⁡(h)\mathcal{R}(h) is nearest to Emb⁡(</latent>)\mathrm{Emb}(\texttt{</latent>}), a decision depending on both components, where the backbone produces a hidden state that encodes the exit and HybridLink maps it onto the anchor embedding. HybridSFT therefore supervises the last latent step of each span from both sides. On the HybridLink side, the regression target at this step is Emb⁡(</latent>)\mathrm{Emb}(\texttt{</latent>}), given slightly more weight than the span interior so that the single exit signal is not diluted. On the backbone side, </latent> is also a cross-entropy target predicted from the same hidden state, so the backbone itself learns to signal the exit.

Appendix C Theoretical Analyses of Hybrid Reinforcement Learning

C.1 Formulation of Hybrid Policy Factorization

Following our notation in Algorithm 1, denote τ=(z,y,o)\tau=(z,y,o) as a hybrid trajectory, where 𝒯\mathcal{T} is the set of sampled text positions. Here, πθ​(τ∣x)\pi_{\theta}(\tau\mid x) denotes the likelihood of the agent’s outputs along trajectory τ\tau, given input xx. Meanwhile, tool observations are generated by the environment and serve as context for subsequent model decisions. We formalize the factorization of the hybrid policy below.

Proposition C.1 (Restatement of Hybrid Policy Factorization).

Let τ\tau be a hybrid trajectory generated by the policy πθ\pi_{\theta} (induced by fθf_{\theta}) with fixed ℛ\mathcal{R}. Then the hybrid policy factorizes as:

πθ​(τ∣x)=∏t∈𝒯πθ​(yt∣x,τ<t),\pi_{\theta}(\tau\mid x)\;=\;\prod_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\pi_{\theta}\bigl(y_{t}\mid x,\,\tau_{<t}\bigr), (13)

where 𝒯\mathcal{T} is the set of sampled text positions of trajectory τ\tau.

Proof.

Fix θ\theta and a realized trajectory τ\tau. At a latent continuation, we have Pr⁡(et=ℛ⁡(ht−1)∣x,τ<t)=1\Pr(e_{t}=\mathcal{R}(h_{t-1})\mid x,\tau_{<t})=1 with a fixed HybridLink ℛ\mathcal{R}. Deterministic reasoning mode transitions (without sampling) also have conditional mass 11. The probability chain rule thus gives

πθ(τ∣x)=[∏t∈𝒯πθ(yt∣x,τ<t)][∏t:deterministicsteps1]=∏t∈𝒯πθ(yt∣x,τ<t),\pi_{\theta}(\tau\mid x)=\left[\prod_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,\tau_{<t})\right]\left[\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}t:\,\text{deterministic}\\ \text{steps}\end{subarray}}1\right]=\prod_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,\tau_{<t}),

where deterministic steps receive the probability of 11.

∎

Remark C.2.

Proposition C.1 shows that the hybrid policy factorizes over sampled text positions, with each text-token probability conditioned on the complete preceding hybrid context, including text, latent thoughts, and tool observations. Building on this factorization formulation, we show in the next subsection (Theorem C.3) how exact rollout replay enables HybridRL’s policy updates to assign credit to complete recorded hybrid trajectories.

C.2 Hybrid Policy Optimization

Recall that we collect {τi=(zi,yi,oi)}i=1G\{\tau_{i}=(z_{i},y_{i},o_{i})\}_{i=1}^{G}, with group size G≥2G\geq 2, using the rollout policy πθold\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}. During replay, πθ​(yi,t∣x,τi,<t)\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t}\mid x,\tau_{i,<t}) scores the recorded prefix with the current model across step tt; πθ​(τi∣x)\pi_{\theta}(\tau_{i}\mid x) is the product in Eq. 13 under this same evaluation. Let ri=r⁡(τi)r_{i}=r(\tau_{i}) be the reward, and AiA_{i} be the fixed group-normalized advantage. Let 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i} denote the sampled text positions of τi\tau_{i}. Define

ρi,t​(θ)\displaystyle\rho_{i,t}(\theta) =πθ​(yi,t∣x,τi,<t)πθold​(yi,t∣x,τi,<t),\displaystyle=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t}\mid x,\tau_{i,<t})}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(y_{i,t}\mid x,\tau_{i,<t})}, (14)
ℒRL​(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RL}}(\theta) =−1∑i|𝒯i|∑i∑t∈𝒯imin{ρi,t(θ)Ai,clip(ρi,t(θ))Ai}.\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\sum_{i}|\mathcal{T}_{i}|}\sum_{i}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{i}}\min\!\left\{\rho_{i,t}(\theta)A_{i},\operatorname{clip}(\rho_{i,t}(\theta))A_{i}\right\}. (15)

Here, clip⁡(ρ)\operatorname{clip}(\rho) restricts ρ\rho to [1−ϵ,1+ϵ][1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon], where 0<ϵ<10<\epsilon<1. Thus, ratios sufficiently close to 11 are unchanged: clip⁡(ρ)=ρ\operatorname{clip}(\rho)=\rho whenever |ρ−1|<ϵ|\rho-1|<\epsilon. In the following theorem, we connect this objective to our hybrid policy optimization over complete recorded hybrid trajectories.

Theorem C.3 (Gradient Equivalence in Hybrid Policy Optimization).

Based on the rollout replay (Section 4.2), record each trajectory’s latent inputs and tool observations. Under Theorem A.1 and the replay conditions in Algorithm 1, the accumulated text-token gradient is equivalent to the advantage-weighted likelihood gradient for the complete hybrid trajectories:

−∇θℒRL​(θold)=1∑i|𝒯i|​∑iAi​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(τi∣x)|θ=θold.-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RL}}(\theta_{\mathrm{old}})=\left.\frac{1}{\sum_{i}|\mathcal{T}_{i}|}\sum_{i}A_{i}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(\tau_{i}\mid x)\right|_{\theta=\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}. (16)

Therefore, the text-token update assigns advantage-weighted policy credit to optimize the complete recorded hybrid trajectories.

Remark C.4.
